etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English insistence, derived from Old French insister (“to insist”). Compare Middle French insistance.

Morphologically insist +‎ -ence.

quote.citation: 1920, Edward Carpenter, Pagan and Christian Creeds, New York: Harcourt, Brace and Co., published 1921, page 72:
quote.text: He made gourd-rattles (known in ever so many parts of the world) in which he rattled dried seeds or small pebbles with a most beguiling and rain-like insistence[.]

quote.citation: 1950 March, H. A. Vallance, “On Foot Across the Forth Bridge”, in Railway Magazine, page 147:
quote.text: The extreme depth of these channels, and the insistence of the Board of Trade on a headway of 150 ft. for the unrestricted passage of large ships, necessitated a high bridge with two main spans, and a central pier on Inchgarvie.

definitions.definition: (fencing) The forcing of an attack through the parry, using strength.
